newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists keep up boycott of parliament.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists keep up boycott of parliament.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament failed to convene for a second day on Friday because of a boycott by deputies of the majority Socialist party protesting at a decision to call an early general election.
The parliamentary leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), Yordan Sokolov, asked for an extraordinary session for Tuesday.

The session would discuss amendments to the electoral law and the income tax law, and a bill giving a mandate to the caretaker cabinet to borrow funds for grain imports and negotiate with the International Monetary Fund.
National radio said Friday's session was declared inquorate because deputies of the Democratic Left coalition arrived at parliament but refused to register in the debating hall.
Socialist party sources said on Thursday they planned to block all activity of the outgoing parliament, due to be dissolved by President Petar Stoyanov this month ready for elections in April.

The Socialists, who won elections in 1994 but lost public support as economic crisis deepened, say they have been removed from power by undemocratic means and should be allowed to complete their parliamentary term.

"I do not see any logic in the Socialists opposing the proposed changes to the income tax law because it is obvious that with this rate of inflation this law should be updated," UDF deputy Assen Agov told Reuters.

"As for our proposal to approve powers for the caretaker government to negotiate loans with international financial institutions, I have to admit that I am not very optimistic that this proposal will be approved by the majority."
The Socialists have said they will attend the session which debates changes in the electoral law.
After 30 days of mass street protests fuelled by economic hardship, Stoyanov on Tuesday brokered a deal under which the Socialists agreed to give up attempts to form a government.

Stoyanov must appoint a caretaker cabinet which must try to keep the economy afloat and organise the elections. Sofia's respected UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski is expected to be named caretaker prime minister.

Most strikes and protests ended after the agreement was announced, but state radio and television are keeping up industrial action to demand an end to censorship, higher wages and the resignation of their directors, who were elected in 1995 by the Socialist-dominated parliament.
National television has stopped showing films, and on Thursday night's main news the newsreader was shown in a long shot instead of the usual closeup.

National radio played an instrumental version of the Beatles' song "Let it Be", before and after every news. Despite the acceptance of suffering advocated by its lyrics, the song became an anthem of anti-communist protesters in 1990.
Between bursts of "Let it Be", jazz replaced the usual output of pop and Bulgarian folk music, but better music provided little comfort for Bulgarians struggling with shortages and soaring prices.
Bread and petrol are in short supply and foreign cigarettes have disappeared because suppliers are reluctant to buy for dollars then sell in the collapsing local currency.

The plummeting lev fell to 3,150-3,000 to the dollar on Friday, compared to about 600 at the beginning of the year. The biggest refinery is running out of imported crude as government price revisions cannot keep up with the fall in the lev.
